Corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy are included as they frequently overlap clinically with bvFTD and may present with behavioral changes before overt parkinsonism or gaze palsy; both are tauopathies with frontostriatal involvement. Early-onset Alzheimer disease is less likely given the prominence of behavioral and disinhibitory symptoms over amnesia, though atypical presentations occur. CTE is considered due to potential exposure history (not provided), but lacks corroborating evidence (e.g., repetitive head trauma history, characteristic imaging or biomarkers) and is lower confidence without supporting context."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD)", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Primary progressive aphasia (non-fluent variant with behavioral features)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Late-onset bipolar I disorder, manic episode with psychotic features", "confidence": 0.42}, {"diagnosis": "Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)", "confidence": 0.38}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.612, "reasoning": "The core presentation—progressive disinhibition (inappropriate laughter, foul language, impulsive grabbing), executive dysfunction, and worsening instrumental activities of daily living with emerging memory impairment—is highly characteristic of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), the most common FTLD syndrome; its insidious onset over months and lack of acute confounders strongly support this (confidence 0.92). CTE is plausible given the behavioral dysexecutive profile and impulsivity, but requires documented repetitive head trauma history—which is unspecified here—making it less certain (0.78). Non-fluent variant PPA can rarely present with prominent behavioral features overlapping bvFTD, especially early in disease, though language deficits are typically more salient; included as a lower-probability mimic (0.65). Late-onset mania is less likely: new-onset mania at this age is rare, usually presents with elevated mood, grandiosity, and hyperactivity—not primarily disinhibition with functional decline—and lacks the progressive neurodegenerative trajectory implied by worsening self-care (0.42). NPH is considered due to the triad of gait disturbance (not reported but often precedes other symptoms), incontinence (not mentioned), and cognitive decline—but the prominent early disinhibition and absence of classic gait or urinary symptoms make it unlikely without further evidence (0.38). Diagnostic uncertainty reflects moderate entropy due to non-negligible probabilities assigned to CTE and PPA, tempering the dominance of bvFTD."}
